newsitem.title: UK: Regulator authorises Britain's first OEIC fund.
newsitem.headline: Regulator authorises Britain's first OEIC fund.

text.p: Britain's Securities and Investment Board said on Wednesday it had authorised Global Asset Management (GAM) Funds as the country's first Open Ended Investment Company (OEIC), and expected more to follow in coming months.
The first sub-fund of the umbrella company is the GAM Japan Growth Fund, and the SIB said the move marked an important step in the development of the UK collective investment schemes industry.
"The establishment of the regulatory framework for OEICs enables the industry to offer new-style collective investment vehicles, which will be marketable across the EU and beyond," the SIB said.

OEICs can be marketed from Britain into Europe under the 1985 Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) directive, which allows for cross-border operation of such funds.
The concept of UCITS was introduced to allow fund management groups in one European Union state to market its product to investors in other countries, provided they meet local marketing requirements.

OEICs are closely modelled on UK unit trusts, but have some critical differences. They will offer a single mid-market price rather than a bid-offer spread, and a corporate structure will allow them to borrow.
They were devised to pull more retail investors into the collective investment market and allow British based fund managers to market a more familiar fund structure in Europe.
Regulations for OEICs came into effect in January.
GAM Funds is an umbrella company under the SIB's regulations. It will consist of a number of sub-funds, in which property is pooled separately.
Initially, it will consist of the single sub-fund investing in Japan.
An SIB spokeswoman said there were several applications for OEIC status in the pipeline, but could not give further details.

Proposals will be published later this month on how the SIB intends to regulate the second stage of OEICS, including derivatives funds, property funds and funds of funds, which have wider investment powers than those available under the regime put in place in January.
Implementation of these proposals is subject to legislation being approved by parliament.
